From 2018 to 2021, DWS made materially misleading statements about its controls for incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into research and investment recommendations for ESG‑integrated products.

DWS marketed itself as a ‘leader in ESG’ and stated that ESG was in its ‘DNA’, yet the firm failed to adequately implement its ESG integration policy and failed to adopt and implement policies and procedures to ensure that its public statements about its ESG integration were accurate.

The first poster featured an aerial image of waves crashing on a shore with text that stated ‘Climate change doesn’t do borders. Neither do rising sea levels. That’s why HSBC is aiming to provide up to $1 trillion in financing and investment globally to help our clients transition to net zero’.

The second poster featured an image of tree growth rings with text that stated ‘Climate changes doesn’t do borders. So in the UK, we’re helping to plant 2 million trees which will lock in 1.25 million tonnes of carbon over their lifetime’.
The CAP Code required that the basis of environmental claims must be clear and that unqualified claims could mislead if they omit significant information.

HSBC UK Bank plc said it had been making the claim in ad (a) since 2020 and aimed to meet the ambition to provide financing and investment globally to help some of its clients transition to net zero by 2030.

HSBC said that the financing of greenhouse gas‑emitting industries was required during the transition to net zero, and so their continued financing of those industries was not in conflict with the aims of a transition to net zero.

We are changing for a cleaner future; to keep the Netherlands warm, operational and moving, Shell is active in oil and gas, but we are changing for a cleaner future; we have to, we can and we want to; therefore, Shell also invests in new energy for the Netherlands, for example through electric transport, hydrogen and biofuels.
We are building wind turbine parks at sea, with smart extras to generate electricity even when the wind isn’t strong; this allows us to make green energy from wind at sea for homes and businesses.

The original complaint against Shell’s statements was that they were in breach of Article 3.1 and 3.2 of the Dutch Sustainability Claims Code, which requires sustainability claims to be clear, specific, correct and unambiguous and prohibits advertising an aspiration when it cannot reasonably be suspected that this will be attained.

Shell breached these requirements with its statements, as Shell’s plans to reduce the production of fossil fuels have been reversed, its investments in renewable energy are only a small fraction of its total budget, and its advertised ‘sustainable’ actions contribute little to nothing to reducing Shell’s emissions.

However, the Advertising Code Committee decided that Shell’s advertisements made sufficiently clear that Shell’s efforts were mere aspirations, as required under Article 3.2 SCC, and argued that it was clear on the face of the advertisements that Shell is in a transition process and that their plans haven’t yet come to fruition.

By failing to apply Article 3.1 SCC, the Committee didn’t test whether Shell’s advertisements were sufficiently substantiated, nuanced and specified; Shell provides no context as to what it means to be ‘changing’ or to become ‘cleaner’.
Board of Appeal decision
You cannot advertise an aspiration when it cannot reasonably be suspected that this will be attained.
It is argued that the Committee overestimates the knowledgeability of the regular consumer regarding Shell’s activities.
The Board of Appeal disagreed with the appellant that Shell’s advertisements would confuse a regular consumer as to what Shell’s operations entail.

Merck’s board of directors oversees ESG matters and has established a cross‑functional EHS Council composed of senior leaders to manage climate‑related issues; the company applies scenario analysis using the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 scenario to assess physical risks for ten key facilities across various hazards.
Governance and risk management

Merck’s risk management process includes identifying, assessing and managing climate‑related risks across at least ten facilities using advanced modelling to evaluate hazards like high temperature, wildfires, drought, storm surge and sea level rise, with results informing adaptation measures and investment decisions.

Banner Bank has established board‑level oversight of climate‑related risks with a risk committee that reviews policies and risk assessments, and its directors receive ESG training to ensure adequate understanding of climate risk and opportunities.

AT&T aims to reduce absolute Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by 2030 from a 2015 baseline and achieve net‑zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2035; by 2022 its emissions were approximately 4.8 million metric tonnes of CO2e, a reduction of over 4 million metric tonnes from 2015 (over 45%).
AT&T aims for 50% of suppliers to set science‑based targets by 2024 and reported that 53% of suppliers had done so by 2022.

AT&T’s Gigaton Goal aims to enable its customers to save 1 billion metric tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, and by 2022 the company reported that customers had avoided 149.2 million metric tonnes through its products and services.

Liberty Mutual continues research and investment in enhancing its modelling capabilities, building a bespoke portfolio‑level transition risk model that leverages NGFS data and advancing insights on high‑priority perils including hurricane frequency, flood and wildfire risk.

Liberty Mutual shares its expertise on managing physical climate risk through the publication of a Physical Climate Risk Management Framework and by hosting the Geneva Association’s Climate Change and Environment Conference to facilitate industry‑wide dialogue on climate.

Liberty Mutual has expanded its Climate Activation Programme globally with new leadership participation, tailored sessions to engage product leaders and the development of new content and online training modules.
